'''Gordon Douglas Slade''' (born December 14, 1955, in [[Toronto]]) is a Canadian mathematician, specializing in [[probability theory]].<ref>{{Scopus id }}</ref><ref name=whoswho>{{Who's Who | author=Anon| title=Slade, Prof. Gordon Douglas | id = U289270 | year = 2018 | doi =10.1093/ww/9780199540884.013.U289270 | edition = online [[Oxford University Press]]|location=Oxford}}</ref>

==Education ==
Slade received in 1977 his bachelor's degree from the [[University of Toronto]] and in 1984 his PhD for research supervised by [[Joel Feldman]] and Lon Rosen at the [[University of British Columbia]].<ref name=mathgene>{{MathGenealogy}}</ref>

==Career and Research ==
As a [[postdoc]] he was a lecturer at the [[University of Virginia]]. From 1986 he was at [[McMaster University]] and since 1999 he is a professor at the University of British Columbia.

He developed the technique of ''lace expansion'' (originally introduced by [[David Brydges]] and [[Thomas Spencer (mathematical physicist)|Thomas C. Spencer]] in 1985) with applications to probability theory and [[statistical mechanics]], such as [[self-avoiding walk|self-avoiding random walks]] and their enumeration, [[random graph]]s, [[percolation theory]], and branched polymers.

In 1989 Slade proved with Takashi Hara that the [[Michael Aizenman|Aizenman]]–[[Charles M. Newman|Newman]] triangle condition at critical percolation is valid in sufficiently high dimension. The Hara–Slade result has important consequences in [[mean field theory]].<ref>Hara, Slade ''The triangle condition for percolation'', Bulletin of the AMS, vol. 21, 1989, pp. 269–273</ref>

In 1991 Slade and Hara used the lace expansion to prove that the average distance covered in self-avoiding random walks in 5 or more dimension grows as the square root of the number of steps and that the scaling limit is [[Wiener process|Brownian motion]].<ref>Hara, Slade ''Critical behaviour of self-avoiding walk in five and more dimensions'', Bulletin of the AMS, vol. 25, 1991, pp. 417–423</ref>

===Honours and awards===

Slade was an invited speaker in 1994 at the ICM in Zürich with lecture ''The critical behaviour of random systems''.

Slade received in 1995 the [[Coxeter–James Prize]]<ref>{{cite web |url=https://personal.math.ubc.ca/~slade/coxeter-james.pdf|title =Laudatio Coxeter–James Prize}}</ref> and in the 2010 the [[CRM-Fields-PIMS Prize]]. He was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society of Canada]] (FRSC) in 2000,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://science.ubc.ca/research/awards|title=Awards and Accolades|date=24 October 2014}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://rsc-src.ca/en/search-fellows?keywords_44=&first_name=gordon&last_name=slade&display_name=&election_year_21=&academy_25=All&division_24=All&discipline_23=All&is_deceased=0&sort_by=last_name&sort_order=ASC|title=Search Fellows}}</ref> in 2010 of the [[Fields Institute]], and in 2012 of the [[American Mathematical Society]] and of the [[Institute of Mathematical Statistics]]. He was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] in 2017.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/gordon-slade-13422/|title=Gordon Slade|publisher=Royal Society|accessdate=28 May 2017|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20170523130447/https://royalsociety.org/people/gordon-slade-13422/|archivedate=23 May 2017}}</ref>  In 2018 Slade was awarded the [[Jeffery–Williams Prize]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Jeffery-Williams Prize|url=https://cms.math.ca/awards/jeffery-williams-prize/|access-date=2021-04-13|website=CMS-SMC|language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=2018|title=Jeffery-Williams Prize|url=https://cms.math.ca/wp-content/uploads/awards/citations/jw2018.pdf|access-date=13 Apr 2021}}</ref>
